headline: The AI evidence gap: security, robotics and trust
subtitle: Original analytical reading exercise based on attributed RSS headlines; source summaries are not independently verified.
editorial_notice: Source-linked, educational reading exercise; RSS headlines and short descriptions have not been independently fact-checked.
essay: The latest wave of artificial-intelligence reporting poses a deceptively difficult question: how much can readers infer from an announcement before examining the evidence behind it? For a technology whose ambitions extend from research laboratories to ordinary workplaces, the distinction matters. A headline may identify an important development, yet the consequences it appears to promise remain provisional until their scope, limitations and practical relevance have been established. Today's selection is therefore best read not as a catalogue of breakthroughs but as an invitation to examine how technological claims acquire credibility.

Security research and practical deployment intersect in The Verge AI's account of Anthropic's free security scans for open-source projects [S1]. The summary identifies a service called OSS Scanner, whose stated purpose is to help detect vulnerabilities. Yet availability alone tells us little about accuracy: even if a tool identifies genuine weaknesses, developers must still distinguish useful alerts from false positives. What evidence would demonstrate that it improves security in practice?

MIT Technology Review strikes a more sceptical note in its discussion of advances in robotics [S2]. The article's headline questions whether apparent breakthroughs will soon transform everyday life, while the supplied excerpt describes the attention attracted by a humanoid robot. Although striking demonstrations can make progress seem immediate, the distinction between performance in controlled settings and dependable use beyond them deserves scrutiny. The excerpt does not establish how widely any capability has been tested.

A question of governance, rather than raw capability, runs through TechCrunch AI's account of Anthropic's revised usage rules [S3]. The source describes restrictions addressing abusive treatment of Claude and election interference, alongside other sensitive forms of misuse. Rules may reveal a company's intentions, but their practical impact depends on enforcement and interpretation. Unless the policy's application can be examined, neither its protective value nor its possible limitations should be taken for granted.

The arXiv preprint on AdaGuard [S4] introduces a different response to safety concerns: a proposed system that uses reasoning-enabled model assessment to apply policies. Its abstract frames the challenge as one of adapting safeguards to changing rules and circumstances. Even so, a proposal described in a preprint should not be equated with independently demonstrated effectiveness. Comparative testing, transparency and the treatment of failures would be essential questions for further reading.

Seen side by side, these accounts resist a single, uncomplicated verdict. Some titles emphasise possibility; others draw attention to constraints, institutional choices or unresolved risks. Although such distinctions can sharpen a reader's sense of what is at stake, they cannot substitute for checking how claims were obtained. A commercial announcement, for example, may establish what an organisation says it intends to offer without showing how reliably the product works in different settings. Equally, a research abstract may describe a promising method without demonstrating that its findings will generalise beyond the conditions in which it was evaluated.

A cautious stance is not the same as blanket scepticism. The former asks what would count as convincing evidence; the latter risks rejecting evidence before considering it. Readers should therefore distinguish a source's stated claim, the supporting information actually supplied, and any wider interpretation they themselves add. Where the description is abbreviated, the appropriate response is to acknowledge uncertainty rather than conceal it behind impressive terminology. This method of reading also helps reveal the writer's tone: measured and inquisitive rather than triumphalist or dismissive.

Ultimately, understanding AI news requires more than recognising prominent companies or technical terms. The most defensible judgement is often provisional: it identifies what can presently be said, specifies what cannot, and explains which further facts might alter the conclusion. Consulting the linked originals matters precisely because the short extracts used here cannot settle those questions. A reader who can distinguish evidence from implication has gained something more enduring than another list of headlines: a way to evaluate tomorrow's news as well.

practice.label: HKDSE Paper 1 Part B2-style practice
practice.instructions: Independent exercises inspired by HKEAA assessment skills, not official exam questions.

items.stem: Which statement best conveys the central argument of the passage?
options: All technological announcements should be rejected.
A headline alone cannot establish the full significance of a development.
Only academic research can provide reliable information.
Newspapers and technology companies have identical purposes.
items.explanation: The opening and conclusion distinguish announcements from independently supported conclusions.

items.stem: In the final paragraph, 'provisional' is closest in meaning to ...
items.explanation: A provisional judgement can change when further evidence emerges.

items.stem: What can reasonably be inferred from the comparison between a commercial announcement and a research abstract?
options: An intention is identical to demonstrated effectiveness.
Different sources require different forms of supporting evidence.
Research abstracts should never be consulted.
items.explanation: The examples highlight distinct gaps in the available evidence.

items.stem: How would you best describe the writer’s attitude towards the reports?
items.explanation: Language including qualified, uncertain and measured expresses caution.

items.stem: Identify TWO reasons why a reader should avoid treating an RSS summary as conclusive evidence. Answer in your own words.
guidance: 1 mark for each distinct valid reason supported by the passage.
Examples: missing methods, shortened context, uncertain outcomes, no independent testing.

items.stem: Explain how the writer uses contrast to develop the argument. Refer to ONE relevant comparison.
guidance: 1 mark: identify a contrast such as announcement versus proven outcome.
1 mark: explain its relevance to careful interpretation.

items.stem: Compare the information in [S1] and [S2]. What can be inferred, and what cannot be concluded without further verification? (60–90 words.)
guidance: 2 marks: accurately explain the focus of the two sources.
1 mark: coherent comparison using both source references.
1 mark: identify a meaningful uncertainty without inventing findings.
items.evidence: First two attributed story paragraphs and the linked original reporting
